title: ECT Parameters
neuronSimIntro: A cross-section through scalp, skull and cortex under the two electrodes, showing how the stimulus parameters act on six pyramidal neurons. Most of the current is shunted through the scalp; only a small part reaches the cortex. Current sets how deep neurons reach threshold, pulse width how long each pulse charges the membrane, frequency how often pulses arrive (also during the refractory period) and duration how long the train lasts. Each pulse alternates polarity: under the anode (+) the cell bodies are depolarized and under the cathode (−) hyperpolarized, so the two sides take turns. Click a neuron to show its membrane potential.
neuronSimFigure: Figure: top, the device current (positive pulses blue, negative purple). Middle, a cross-section through scalp, skull, cerebrospinal fluid and cortex under electrodes E1 and E2, with the current paths (most of the current is shunted through the scalp) and six pyramidal neurons: 1-3 under E1 and 4-6 under E2, with 1 and 6 nearest the electrodes, 2 and 5 in the middle and 3 and 4 farthest away. Bottom, the membrane potential of the selected neuron (click a neuron or use the buttons below). Neurons turn orange when depolarized and blue when hyperpolarized; under the anode the cell bodies are depolarized, so the two sides take turns as the pulses alternate. Schematic model (leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with refractory period and strength-duration relation), shown in slow motion; illustration only, not a quantitative prediction. How frequency affects seizure induction in patients cannot be derived from a single neuron's refractory period alone.
simPhasePos: Positive pulse: E1 anode (+), E2 cathode (−)
simPhaseNeg: Negative pulse: E1 cathode (−), E2 anode (+)
singleTitle: Action potential in a single neuron
singleIntro: One neuron during one pulse with the settings above, in slow motion, after the Hodgkin-Huxley model (squid axon parameters, time-compressed so that the chronaxie is 0.25 ms; illustration only): the membrane with voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, next to the membrane potential with its phases numbered as in the figure caption. Choose a neuron farther from the electrode to see its higher threshold.
saltatoryIntro: The device's pulse train is applied at one end of a myelinated axon and spreads by saltatory conduction: myelin insulates the internodes, and the action potential is regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier, where voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are concentrated, so it jumps from node to node with unchanged amplitude. At a low dose only the nearest node reaches threshold and the rest are excited by conduction; a longer pulse or higher current widens the directly excited stretch but not the action potential, which is all-or-none. Far from the electrode the stimulus stays subthreshold and the passive depolarization fades along the axon. At high frequency pulses can fall in the refractory period and fail, and negative pulses hyperpolarize the membrane (after Purves et al., Neuroscience, 6th ed.).
apFigureCaption: Figure: the membrane with voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, and the membrane potential during one pulse, with the phases numbered. At rest the inside is negative (−65 mV): Na⁺ is concentrated outside and K⁺ inside, gradients kept by the pump. (1) Depolarization: the stimulus current charges the membrane and the potential rises. (2) Threshold: Na⁺ channels open fast enough that Na⁺ inflow exceeds K⁺ and leak outflow; from here the action potential is all-or-none. (3) Rising phase: positive feedback opens more Na⁺ channels and Na⁺ rushes in toward E(Na⁺) = +50 mV. (4) Peak: the inside is positive, Na⁺ channels inactivate (ball and chain) and K⁺ channels open. (5) Falling phase: K⁺ flows out and the membrane repolarizes. (6) Undershoot: K⁺ channels close slowly, so the potential dips below rest toward E(K⁺) = −77 mV before it returns. During the absolute refractory period (red) no new action potential can start; during the relative one (orange) a stronger stimulus is needed. If the stimulus does not reach threshold (a short pulse, low current or a neuron far from the electrode), the membrane only charges and discharges without an action potential.
condTitle: Pulse train along a myelinated axon
condSummary: Figure: top, the stimulus at the axon (yellow) with the threshold for the present pulse width (red); nodes under the orange part are excited directly. Middle, the membrane potential at each node of Ranvier from −0.1 to 6 ms after the first excitatory pulse; orange traces are nodes excited directly, black traces nodes reached by saltatory conduction, later the farther they lie from the electrode. Bottom, the highest and lowest potential along the axon in the first {w} ms. The buttons under Neuron stimulation choose how far the neuron lies from the electrode and under which electrode the axon lies. The electrodes swap roles with each pulse: under {el} the {sign} pulses excite, while the others hyperpolarize here and instead excite axons under {other}. With {pw} ms, {i} mA and {f} Hz and the neuron {where}, {ok} of {pos} excitatory pulses reached threshold, giving {aps} action potentials from {n} pulses; {direct} of {nodes} nodes were excited directly.
condMiddle: at a middle distance from the electrode

synNoRelease: No action potential: no neurotransmitter is released.
synIntro: At the axon terminal the electrical signal is passed on chemically. The action potential opens Ca²⁺ channels, Ca²⁺ triggers the release of transmitter, and the transmitter opens receptor channels in the postsynaptic membrane, where it gives an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP). One synapse gives only a few millivolts; it is the sum of many synapses active at the same time that brings the next neuron to threshold, which is why the synchronous activity started by the ECT stimulus can spread through the network (after Purves et al., Neuroscience, 6th ed.).
synEpspAxis: Time after arrival at the terminal (ms)
synFigureCaption: Figure: a myelinated axon ends in a presynaptic terminal on a postsynaptic dendrite; the numbers follow the sequence of chemical transmission. (1) Transmitter is synthesized and stored in vesicles. (2) An action potential invades the terminal, and (3) the depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the active zone, so that (4) Ca²⁺ flows in. (5) Ca²⁺ makes vesicles fuse with the membrane, and (6) the transmitter, here glutamate, is released into the cleft by exocytosis. (7) It binds to receptors in the postsynaptic density, and (8) these ligand-gated cation channels (AMPA type) open: Na⁺ flows in, more than K⁺ flows out. (9) The net inward current spreads along the dendrite and depolarizes it: an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP). The EPSP is graded, a few millivolts from one synapse, and fades within milliseconds (dashed curve); when many synapses are active at once their EPSPs sum, and if the sum reaches threshold at the axon hillock an action potential starts in the postsynaptic cell (solid curve). (10) The vesicle membrane is retrieved by clathrin-coated endocytosis and refilled. In ECT the stimulus excites many neurons at once, and this synchronous synaptic drive spreads through the network as the seizure.
